1uczau0: “Ni… ni”: ruling out two things at once
1jy12el: “Ni… ni” denies two elements at the same time: “El hostal no tenía ni wifi ni agua caliente”. If the sentence starts with “no”, the first “ni” is optional in some cases, but with “ni… ni” the idea is clearer. If “ni… ni” comes at the start, before the verb, you don’t need “no”: “Ni el precio ni el horario son un problema”.
1urjnqm: With two singular subjects before the verb, the plural is normal: “Ni el guía ni el conductor hablaban inglés”. It also works to rule out two explanations or two options: “No fue ni por la lluvia ni por el tráfico”.
dighih: There were neither clean sheets nor towels.
10gry6y: Neither the bus nor the train goes as far as the village.
1dp5p2g: Before the verb: no “no” and in the plural.
zs6ll9: I don’t want coffee or tea, thanks.
8mjb7s: With “ni” you repeat “ni”: it isn’t mixed with “o”.
1phg57a: If “ni… ni” goes before the verb, “no” is not added.
12w3149: Pero, sin embargo and aunque: the weight of the ending
lh71ib: “Pero” joins two opposing ideas within one sentence: “El trayecto es largo, pero el paisaje es increíble”. “Sin embargo” does the same with more force and usually starts a new sentence or goes between commas: “El hostal era barato. Sin embargo, las camas eran muy incómodas”. It can also go inside the second idea: “El desayuno, sin embargo, era excelente”.
1jazugs: “Aunque” can add a short reservation at the end, often with just an adjective: “Es una excursión cansada, aunque muy bonita”. Remember the golden rule: what comes last weighs more. “Es bonito, aunque caro” leaves an impression of “caro”; “Es caro, aunque bonito” leaves an impression of “bonito”.
1d3e91o: Before closing your opinion, decide what you want the reader to remember and put it at the end.
11zg0s: Three ways to add a counterweight
c6a6d1: “Sin embargo” goes after a full stop or semicolon, and has a comma after it.
ds7ftx: Porque, como and es que: causes in conversation
djzbdd: “Porque” goes after the result and answers “¿por qué?”: “Llegamos tarde porque el bus se averió”. In a short answer it can stand alone: “¿Por qué no fuiste? — Porque estaba enfermo”. “Como”, for its part, always goes at the beginning, before the result: “Como el bus se averió, llegamos tarde”.
oh0153: “Es que” is very colloquial: it presents a cause as an excuse or explanation when someone asks you to account for something: “Perdona el retraso, es que no encontraba las llaves”. And “por” + noun or infinitive gives the cause briefly: “Cerraron por la nieve”, “Perdón por llegar tarde”.
ejxl9x: As there were no seats on the bus, we rented a car.
1wkkuce: “Como” at the start of the sentence.
3x69kr: We rented a car because there were no seats on the bus.
1n4r37r: —Aren’t you coming to dinner? —The thing is, I’ve got a headache.
1gbx9i5: Causal “como” only goes at the start of the sentence.
155els: After “por” comes an infinitive or a noun, not a conjugated verb.
sz2uz8: Ya que, puesto que, debido a, gracias a and por culpa de
fxlliu: “Ya que”, “puesto que” and “dado que” present a cause the listener already knows or accepts. They are more formal than “porque” and can go at the start or after, with a comma: “Puesto que la carretera está cerrada, la excursión se aplaza”, “La excursión se aplaza, ya que la carretera está cerrada”.
nkks4p: “Debido a” and “a causa de” go with a noun and are typical of notices and news: “debido a la nieve”. If a conjugated verb follows, you need “que”: “debido a que nevó”. Finally, “gracias a” presents a cause with a positive result and “por culpa de”, with a negative result: “Vimos los cóndores gracias al guía”, “Perdimos el bus por culpa del tráfico”.
xjuatt: Ask yourself who you are talking to: with a friend, “como” or “es que”; in a formal email or a notice, “ya que”, “puesto que” or “debido a”.
kw641z: “Debido a” goes with a noun; with a conjugated verb it needs “que”.
m3gex9: The result is negative: “por culpa de” or “a causa de”.

r849nt: Como / cómo, porque / por qué and the pause of “sin embargo”
1vtsk4i: Causal “como” is unstressed: it leans on the next word and is hardly marked (“como‿no había plazas…”). Interrogative “cómo” is stressed: it is said with force and has a written accent (“¿Cómo llegaste?”). The same happens with “porque” (one word, soft stress on “-QUE”: por-QUE) and “por qué” (two words, strong stress on “QUÉ”).
r8jcow: “Sin embargo” usually goes between pauses and with a small change of tone, like a door opening to the opposite idea: “Era caro. | Sin embargo, | valió la pena”. That pause helps the listener notice the counterweight.
dv3cnt: “Porque” (cause) is one word without an accent; “por qué” (question) is two words with an accent; “el porqué” is a noun (“el porqué de la cancelación”). Causal “como” has no accent; “cómo” in questions does.

bqah7l: The second day was the best. We got up early again, although this time for a good reason: at eight, at the Cruz del Cóndor viewpoint, we saw six condors flying very close. Since they don’t always appear, the guide told us we had been very lucky.
